opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core problem we start from is that if you look inside a language model, at the activations of individual neurons, they're pretty hard to make sense of. A single neuron will fire for, say, academic citations, and Korean text, and something about HTTP requests. That's what people call polysemanticity. And the leading hypothesis for why is superposition: the model wants to represent far more concepts than it has dimensions, so it packs them in as directions that aren't perfectly orthogonal, and that works fine as long as any given input only uses a handful of concepts at once.

Sparse coding, or dictionary learning, is basically the tool that takes that hypothesis seriously. You train a sparse autoencoder, or a related setup like a transcoder, on the model's activations. It learns a much larger set of directions, a dictionary of features, maybe millions of them, and it's constrained so that for any given token, only a small number of those features are active, and you can reconstruct the original activation from that sparse combination. Sparsity is the key ingredient. It pushes each feature toward meaning one thing, because the cheapest way to explain the data with few active pieces is to have pieces that line up with the actual underlying concepts.

When it works, you get features that are surprisingly crisp. A feature for the Golden Gate Bridge that fires on text about it, on images of it, in different languages. Features for code bugs, for deception-related concepts, for very specific grammatical structures. You can check them by looking at what activates them, but also causally, by turning a feature up or down and seeing the model's behavior change in the way you'd predict.

I'd add two caveats. First, it's a lens, not ground truth. The dictionary is a model of the model, and there's reconstruction error, so some of what the network computes falls outside what the features capture, and you have to keep track of that. Second, features alone are just a vocabulary. The more exciting part, and much of what we've worked on lately, is using those features as building blocks to trace circuits: how features in one layer combine to produce features in the next, so you can follow the model's actual reasoning on a specific prompt, like seeing it plan a rhyme ahead of time or do a multi-step inference internally. Sparse coding is what makes that possible, because it gives you units you can actually read.

r001.rationale: It describes neurons firing for unrelated concepts and explains that superposition packs many concepts into non-orthogonal directions.

r002.rationale: It says the method learns a much larger dictionary of features from the model’s activations.

r003.rationale: It says only a small number of features are active, but does not explain that a penalty on nonzero code activations encourages this sparsity.

r004.rationale: It says the sparse combination can reconstruct the original activation and mentions reconstruction error, but does not say reconstruction error is used to train the code.

r005.rationale: It says sparsity pushes each feature toward meaning one thing and describes the resulting features as crisp.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. So the starting point is that when you look inside a language model, the thing you'd naively want to do is look at individual neurons and say, okay, this neuron does X. And that basically doesn't work. A single neuron in a model like Claude will fire on a mix of things that seem totally unrelated. It might fire on academic citations, and also on Korean text, and also on some specific kind of HTTP request. There's a word for this, polysemanticity, and it just means that a neuron isn't a clean unit of meaning.

The hypothesis we're working from is that this happens because the model is trying to represent way more concepts than it has neurons. If you have a residual stream of a few thousand dimensions and you need to track millions of distinct ideas, you can't give each idea its own dimension. So the model packs them in as directions that overlap, and each neuron ends up participating in lots of them. That's the superposition idea.

Sparse coding, or what we usually call a sparse autoencoder or a dictionary learning setup, is a way to try to unmix that. You take the activations at some layer of the model, and you train a second, much wider model to reconstruct them. The key constraint is that for any given token, only a small number of the units in that wide model are allowed to be active. So you're saying: express this activation as a sum of a handful of directions pulled from a big dictionary of possible directions, and learn the dictionary so that this works well across a lot of text.

What falls out of that, when it works, is that the individual units in the dictionary tend to be much more interpretable than the raw neurons. You get a unit that fires on the Golden Gate Bridge, and really just that, whether it's in English or Japanese or in an image. Or a unit for code that has a bug in it, or for someone being sycophantic. The sparsity is doing the work there. By forcing the model to explain each activation with only a few parts, you're pushing it to find parts that each carry a coherent piece of meaning, because that's the most efficient way to reconstruct the data under that constraint.

The reason I find this a comprehensibility tool rather than just a compression trick is that it gives you a vocabulary. Before, you had a vector of numbers and no way to talk about it. After, you have a set of named features, and you can ask questions in those terms. What features were active when the model gave this answer? If I turn this feature up, does the behavior change in the way the name predicts? That last part matters a lot. The names we give features are hypotheses, and intervening on them is how you check that the hypothesis is actually about the model and not just a story we told ourselves.

I'd add the usual caveats. The dictionary is not the ground truth, it's a learned approximation, and it misses things. The features you get depend on how wide you make the dictionary, and some of them are still messy. And finding a feature isn't the same as understanding how the model uses it. But as a first step from "a pile of activations" to "a set of concepts you can name and poke at," it's been the most productive thing we've found.

r001.rationale: It explains that concepts overlap in the residual stream, so individual neurons participate in multiple ideas.

r002.rationale: It describes training a much wider model to represent activations as a small number of directions from a larger dictionary.

r003.rationale: It says only a small number of units may be active, but does not explain penalizing nonzero code activations.

r004.rationale: It says the wider model is trained to reconstruct the original activations and to learn a dictionary that does so well across text.

r005.rationale: It describes dictionary units as tending to carry a coherent piece of meaning, with an example that fires on the Golden Gate Bridge.

astra-6.text:
The intuition is that a language model represents many different concepts using the same neurons. So if you look at one neuron and ask, “What does this mean?” you might find that it responds to several seemingly unrelated things. The neuron isn’t necessarily the right unit of explanation.

Sparse coding tries to find a different set of building blocks for those representations. You take the model’s activations and learn to reconstruct them using a much larger collection of features, with the constraint that only a small number of features can be active for any particular input. A sparse autoencoder is one way to do that.

The hope is that those features separate out concepts that are mixed together in the original representation. You can then look at the examples that activate a feature and ask whether there’s a consistent pattern—maybe a topic, a grammatical structure, or something more abstract.

But finding a feature that looks interpretable isn’t the same as understanding the model. You also want to intervene on that feature and see whether it changes the model’s behavior in the way you’d expect. So I think of sparse coding as giving us candidate building blocks that we can inspect and test.

r001.rationale: The response says the same neurons can represent many different concepts, mixing them in the original representation.

r002.rationale: It describes reconstructing the model’s activations using a much larger collection of features.

r003.rationale: It says only a small number of features can be active, but does not explain that a penalty on nonzero code activations encourages this sparsity.

r004.rationale: It says the activations are reconstructed, but does not state that reconstruction error trains the sparse code to preserve information from the original vector.

r005.rationale: It says features may separate mixed concepts and can be inspected for patterns, but does not clearly state that each feature tends to represent a single concept.

sol-6.1.text:
The intuition is that a language model has these internal activations, these vectors of numbers, and we’d like to understand what they represent. You might start by looking at individual neurons, but a neuron can respond to several seemingly unrelated things. So the model’s concepts don’t necessarily line up neatly with its neurons.

Sparse coding gives us another way to describe those activations. We try to reconstruct them using a much larger collection of learned directions, with the constraint that only a small number of those directions are active for any particular input. We call those directions features. The hope is that a feature corresponds to something more understandable, like a particular topic, a grammatical structure, or a pattern in code.

A sparse autoencoder is one way to learn that decomposition. You train it to preserve the original activation while penalizing it for using too many features. Then you can look at examples where each feature activates and ask, ‘What do these examples have in common?’ You can also intervene on a feature and see how that changes the model’s output.

That doesn’t automatically give you a complete explanation of the model. Features can still be ambiguous, and reconstruction can miss information. But it gives you a set of more interpretable building blocks for investigating what the model is doing.

r001.rationale: It says individual neurons can respond to unrelated things, but does not clearly state that a dense activation vector mixes representations of multiple concepts.

r002.rationale: It describes reconstructing activations from a much larger collection of learned directions, which maps them into a higher-dimensional representation.

r003.rationale: It says the sparse autoencoder is penalized for using too many features, so only a small number activate for an input.

r004.rationale: It says training should preserve the original activation, but does not identify reconstruction error as the training signal.

r005.rationale: It says a feature may correspond to an understandable topic or pattern, but does not clearly characterize each feature as tending to represent a single concept.
